analysis: The first option anchors historical art in Western art, Renaissance Italy, African art and heritage, modern art and museums, and historiography. Archaeology contributes artefact description and interpretation. Native American Histories supplies Indigenous historical and cultural expression, and History of Empires supplies cross-regional context. Literary analysis, historical research and ethics support interpretation; they do not become art-history courses.

The second option uses the shared art-history core to support sustained visual media analysis and social inquiry. Television and disability representation, environmental imagery, climate protest art, contemporary social theory and public persuasion distinguish it from the historical and material-culture option. Film, documentary and creative production are direct visual and cultural practice, with stylistics and sociology as supporting methods.

Eight different courses each way yield 60 EC of pairwise difference. Architecture, conservation and museum work inform both concepts, but the workbook has no dedicated cumulative conservation or architecture sequence that would support a third option. Archaeology, art-history surveys and museum interpretation provide partial disciplinary overlap without the comparator’s multi-course techniques, specialist fieldwork or dedicated thesis.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: Provides the modern-period historical context needed to situate nineteenth- and twentieth-century art in social and political change.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.contribution: Examines imperial histories and colonial relations that shape the cross-regional circulation and interpretation of art and heritage.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.contribution: Studies Native American histories and cultural expressions, providing a specific historical context for art and heritage in the Americas.

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: Develops a historical research question, evaluates sources and writes a substantial paper. Supports independent inquiry alongside the Art History courses.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: Studies ethical reasoning that can be applied to ownership, presentation and contested heritage; it is a complementary method, not a museum-studies substitute.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: Introduces sociological theories of how cultural production and media relate to social structures.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: Teaches qualitative research design and interpretation useful for studying audiences, institutions and cultural meaning.

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.contribution: Studies colonialism, modernity and social theory as frames for contemporary visual culture and cultural representation.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: Examines contemporary social theory and civil society, giving conceptual grounding for socially engaged art and media.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: Studies classical rhetoric, argumentation and audience appeal through speeches and an applied storytelling project.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.contribution: Studies how stylistic choices produce meaning in texts, a specific analytic complement to media representation.

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.contribution: Directly analyzes films, exhibitions, protest art and social media in public debate about climate change.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: Studies persuasion across communication and society, complementing analysis of how contemporary visual culture addresses publics.

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.contribution: Studies and creates artistic communication through theory, performance and reflective writing.

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice and develops a researched visual analysis of a painting on location.

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: Studies the making, materiality and interpretation of objects across world regions, complementing art history with archaeological evidence.

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.contribution: Examines African artistic traditions and heritage, extending the historical art curriculum beyond Europe.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: Directly examines Renaissance painting, sculpture and architecture through Mediterranean trade and cross-cultural exchange.

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.contribution: Uses Greek archaeology and material evidence to investigate ancient community life, a specific ancient material-culture complement rather than a survey of ancient art.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.contribution: Directly studies modern art and the curatorial and exhibition choices of modern museums.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.contribution: Investigates the political meanings of ancient heritage and civic memory, a specific complement to heritage interpretation rather than architectural history.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: Traces art history as a discipline through theorists and methods for interpreting meaning, identity and authorship.

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: Interprets major literary works across periods, supplying narrative and cultural contexts for art.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: Examines global myths and narratives that furnish identifiable subjects and interpretive contexts for historical art.

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.contribution: Studies film adaptation from literary texts, connecting cinematic visual form to stories and cultural interpretation.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.contribution: Introduces film history, visual analysis and the development of film as cultural expression.

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.contribution: Studies physical media technologies and their role in cultural production and preservation, adding a material-media perspective to visual culture.

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.contribution: Examines the social history of television and contemporary mainstream media, focusing on who produces and frames public narratives.

MCCMEDI212.name: Media & the Environment
MCCMEDI212.contribution: Analyses how visual, audiovisual and digital media represent ecological problems and influence public understanding.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: Examines how film, photographs and music represent race, memory, power and resistance.

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.contribution: Analyzes the history and visual techniques of documentary film as an artistic and social representation form.

alignment.rationale: Both supply explicit academic-skills preparation; UCR PPD is broader than the programme-specific UvA course.

Both use visual analysis and place artworks in historical context. UvA’s first survey starts in antiquity. UCR starts with late-medieval and Renaissance painting and continues through contemporary art.
Both study how objects are made through material evidence and close observation. UCR uses archaeological artefacts and technical drawings. UvA studies architecture and sculpture.
Both study artistic exchange across regions and the influence of colonialism and collecting. UCR concentrates on African art and heritage. UvA ranges across several continents.
Both study early modern painting, sculpture and architecture. UCR focuses on Renaissance Italy and its trade and cultural connections across the Mediterranean and beyond.
